extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, and researchers seeking career/research advice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians on how to learn, compare, and incorporate mathematical techniques from other subfields into their own work to broaden their research toolkit and improve the quality of their mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn beyond your specialty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians should not become trapped by their own toolkit. When encountering an unfamiliar method, 'try to see whether your own tools can in fact accomplish a similar task.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss unfamiliar techniques out of hand; instead actively attempt to understand them and test whether analogous results can be achieved using your familiar tools. Anti-pattern: remaining siloed in one set of techniques and avoiding engagement with other approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than dismissing other techniques, study 'the simplest model case in which that tool does something non-trivial' to develop a meaningful comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a new tool by identifying minimal/example problems where it is effective; compare those examples to what your current methods can do to understand relative advantages and limitations. Guidance implies hands-on comparison on toy cases rather than relying on vague impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a diverse repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: Through consistent practice, 'add that tool permanently to your repertoire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After learning and testing a method, practice it until it becomes a reliable part of your toolbox. Emphasis on repeated use and integration into one's regular problem-solving habits rather than one-off exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disciplinary study
rubrics_metrics.description: Use survey articles and proceedings (e.g. ICM materials) to understand how other fields approach their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively read broad survey literature and conference proceedings to get high-level views of other subfields' techniques and perspectives. Practical sources recommended include survey articles and ICM (International Congress of Mathematicians) materials as accessible entry points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality marker: external-tool absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' piece of mathematics is one whose author has clearly absorbed tools from outside their immediate area; this shows in proof choice, references, and motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of strong work include evidence that the author used ideas or methods from other areas: deliberate proof choices leveraging external tools, citations to other fields' literature, and motivations framed by cross-disciplinary perspectives. Anti-pattern: work that appears narrowly motivated and uses only in-area heuristics despite availability of broader methods.
